name: Umar Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing law, so I spend a lot of time reading cases about contracts and negligence that are written in a way that's meant to confuse you. I live with my parents and my little sister and commute by tram. Four evenings a week I work in a customer service call centre for a broadband company, answering the phones from six until ten.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you notice about the call centre job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The scripts. Half the calls are the same five problems, and I've got a screen that tells me what to say next. My manager keeps saying the new software will suggest the answer for us, which is helpful, but it also makes me wonder what I'm for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. That one is called AI Plateau. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's okay, a useful helper for some jobs but not the revolution people shout about. At the call centre it already suggests answers, and that's about the limit. I'd say we should carry on and see what turns up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm not scared of AI, I'm scared of my own numbers. My loan is big and my call centre pay is just enough for the tram and lunch. If the company cut hours, I'd have nothing behind me. A law degree with average grades is not an automatic ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the call centre job and aim for a paralegal placement next summer. I'd go to the law society talks and ask older students how they got in. I'd also use AI sometimes for study, like checking my notes, but I'd double-check anything it says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty normal. Not great, not bad. A bit of money worry hums in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the money feel so thin when you live at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because home isn't free in my head. My dad drives a taxi and the fares are dropping, and my mum works at a care home on a zero-hours contract. I don't ask them for anything, so every pound has to come from the phone shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by asking what you are for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a screen tells me what to say, and a customer can only tell the difference by my accent, then a machine could do it. I'm not saying I'm useless, I'm saying the job is already half-automated. I'd rather be doing something that takes judgement.

say: I'd say AI is a **useful helper**, not the revolution people shout about.
I'd say carry on and **see what turns up**.
think: I'm scared of my **own numbers**, not AI: a big loan and thin pay.
A law degree with **average grades** is no automatic ticket.
do: Keep the **call centre job** and aim for a paralegal placement next summer.
Go to **law society talks** and ask older students how they got in.
feel: Pretty **normal**, with a hum of money worry in the background.
S0.quote: My dad drives a taxi and the fares are dropping, and my mum works at a care home on a zero-hours contract.
fieldNote: Umar's money worry is the **household's** as much as his own.
He already sees his call centre job as half-automated.
Won't ask his parents for help, so each pound comes from phone shifts.

steps.text: Keep the four evening call centre shifts
Check my law notes with an AI tool and verify them
Apply for a paralegal placement next summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. That one is called Steady Disruption. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good to be prepared, and some jobs will go while new ones appear. In my call centre they're already training us to work with the software. I'd say, learn the tool, because it's coming either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think the call centre is the first place it hits, and I'm in it. Answering customers is on the list on the card, so those jobs shrink first. As a law student, I'd also see that research and drafting, which is what junior lawyers do, can be done faster by software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get really good at using AI for legal research and writing, and tell the firms that. I'd keep the call centre job for as long as it lasts, but I'd also look for a part-time job in a law office, even filing, to get my foot in. I'd ask my tutor which areas of law are most about talking to people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy but okay. It's the sort of change you can see coming and plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you actually show a law firm that you can use AI well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write up a short case where I used it to summarise a contract and then checked every line myself. A firm wants someone who spots when the machine is wrong. I think that's what they'll pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to you if the call centre cut staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lose roughly half my income. I'd go to my manager before it happened and ask to move to a team that handles complaints, because those need a person. If not, I'd look at warehouse or retail shifts until something better came up.

say: I'd say learn the tool, because it's **coming either way**.
I'd tell friends some jobs go and **new ones appear**.
think: The call centre is **the first place** this hits, and I work there.
Junior legal **research and drafting** could be done faster by software.
do: Get good at AI for **legal research**, checking every line myself.
Find a part-time job in a **law office**, even filing.
feel: A bit **uneasy** but okay, since it can be seen coming and planned for.
S1.quote: A firm wants someone who spots when the machine is wrong. I think that's what they'll pay for.
fieldNote: Umar sees **two exposures**: the call centre now and junior legal work later.
His steady approach is to learn the tool and show his checking.
Has a fallback plan with specific team and shift options.

steps.text: Write a short case study of AI contract summaries I checked
Ask the manager about moving to the complaints team
Look for part-time filing work in a law office

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. That one is called AGI by 2028. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock and we'll all need help. Companies need to slow down and give people notice. I wouldn't say anything dramatic. I'd just say let's see what the government does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think there's no way to finish law and have a career in it. If almost all thinking work is done by AI in 2028, that includes contracts and cases. I'd also lose the call centre job, and that's both of my incomes gone before I qualify.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents the same night. I'd ask the university whether I can switch to a course that leads to something hands-on or in public service. I'd save every pound, and look at a trade or a role in the care home my mum works in, since robots arrive three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty shaken. It's hard to concentrate on contracts when the contract itself is unclear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years, what's your first move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Speak to the university adviser. I'd ask what happens to loan repayments if the jobs vanish, and whether courses can be changed without more debt. I've never asked that sort of question, but I'd do it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your family react?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say work harder, he always does. My mum would worry and say don't make big decisions yet. They'd both be scared but they wouldn't show it, so I'd have to say it for them.

say: I'd say it's a **shock** and companies must give people notice.
I'd say let's see what the **government** does.
think: There may be no way to finish law and have a **career in it**.
I'd lose both the call centre and my **future** job.
do: Ask the university adviser what happens to **loan repayments**.
Look at a **hands-on role** in the care sector like my mum's.
feel: **Shaken**, and hard to focus on contracts.
S2.quote: I'd also lose the call centre job, and that's both of my incomes gone before I qualify.
fieldNote: Umar loses **both incomes** in his own mind: the call centre now, law later.
Plans to ask practical questions about loan repayment.
Knows his parents will hide fear, so he'd have to say it.

steps.text: Ask the university adviser about loan repayments
Look at hands-on care sector jobs like my mum's
Save every pound from the phone shifts
Talk with my parents the same night

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. That one is called AGI by 2031. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to adjust if you start early. I'd tell people not to sit and watch. I'd say the same to my dad, who thinks it's science fiction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel nervous but possible. I'd qualify in three years and have two to find a place before AGI lands. That's tough, but not impossible. I'd think about which parts of law are about people, like family or criminal cases, and aim for those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree and aim for a role with a lot of client contact, maybe in a small firm. I'd keep the call centre while it lasts, then move to a job that needs people. I'd save a little and ask my parents to talk to the bank about their own plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have a plan, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop my pride about asking for help. I'd visit the careers office early, join law society events and ask a lawyer to let me shadow them for a day. I'd also start the saving habit, even ten a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years compare to ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten would feel almost comfortable and I'd probably put things off. Five is the sweet spot for me: close enough that I move now, far enough that I can actually do something about it.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to adjust** if you start early.
I'd tell my dad it isn't **science fiction**.
think: I'd qualify in three years with only **two years** left before it lands.
I'd aim for **client-facing** law, like family or criminal cases.
do: Finish the degree and aim for a **small firm** with client contact.
Visit the **careers office** early and shadow a lawyer for a day.
S3.quote: Five is the sweet spot for me: close enough that I move now, far enough that I can actually do something about it.
fieldNote: Umar finds the **five-year window** motivating rather than frightening.
Wants client-facing work as his hedge.
Admits pride is the thing holding him back from asking for help.

steps.text: Visit the university careers office this term
Ask a local lawyer if I can shadow them for a day
Save ten pounds a week from the phone shifts
Keep the call centre job while it lasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. That one is called AGI by 2036. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway and it would be silly to panic. We should still plan. I'd say that employers and universities need to start teaching the right things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel fairly good about my situation. I'd be twenty-eight, qualified, maybe working at a firm with my loan half paid. I'd worry about prices and rent, but not about being replaced all at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work for a firm, and keep an eye on which kinds of cases AI can't handle. I'd learn the tools properly, probably in the first couple of years of my job. I'd also buy a small flat if I could, because that seems like a good way to be steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. It's a long time and I'm used to taking things step by step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could knock that plan off course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A slow job market or a bad year at home. If my dad stops driving because of an accident, or my mum's care home closes, I'd need to step in. That would matter more than AI, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your little sister that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, you're twelve, so you've got loads of time. Learn to think and ask questions, and don't just follow what the screen says. I'd tell her it's fine to be curious about AI, but not to let it do her homework.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long runway** and panic would be silly.
I'd say employers and universities should **start teaching** the right things.
think: I'd feel **fairly good**: qualified at twenty-eight with half the loan paid.
I'd worry about **prices and rent** more than being replaced.
do: Finish the degree, work for a firm and learn which **cases AI can't handle**.
Learn the tools **properly** in my first couple of years.
feel: **Fairly calm**, since I take things step by step.
S4.quote: If my dad stops driving because of an accident, or my mum's care home closes, I'd need to step in.
fieldNote: Umar's unease comes from **family fragility**, not AI.
His steady personality shows in step-by-step plans.
Would teach his sister to think rather than copy the screen.

steps.text: Finish the law degree and take a firm job
Learn legal AI tools properly in my first years
Pay half the loan down by twenty-eight
Help my parents if the taxi or care job ends

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd lose the call centre and the law career at the same time, and my parents have nothing to catch us. What would help is advice on which jobs last, a government that can pay for retraining, and a loan system that doesn't punish people who change course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being a student at home isn't the same as being comfortable. My dad's fares are dropping and my mum's hours aren't fixed. A lot of us are quietly holding the household together while studying.

headlineQuote: A lot of us are quietly holding the household together while studying.
portrait: Umar, 18, studies **law** and works four evenings in a broadband call centre, living with his parents and sister.
He uses AI now and then, and sees his call centre job as **half-automated** already.
He's a pragmatic centrist who blames no one and plans step by step.
His worry is as much about his parents' shaky work as his own, so even the quiet scenario is anxious.
The two-year warning would take both of his incomes, but five years feels like a workable window.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because the call centre and the law career would go together.
whatWouldHelp: Honest advice on which jobs last, **funded retraining** and a loan system that doesn't punish changing course.
